item.title: Critique
item.content:encoded:
I liked this tale, and I am upvoting because I enjoyed reading it. There was a lot that was good about it, it is a nice silly dystopian tale.

However, there are many errors, some of which I can not fix without changing the meaning of the sentences involved.

See below:
See below:

“Huh, Well I’m jealous.”
Should w be lowercase?

Near the beginning, there should be 3 pieces of toast (the two original slices and the raison slice) but on 2 occasions it is listed as 2 slices of toast (I could joke that Ralph disappeared 1 slice without noticing).
The sentences in question are:
"Ralph placed both slices in the box," and "Two pieces, he could hold both in one hand"
Here are possible ways to fix this:
1. Make there be only one slice on the plate to begin with.
2. Mention that Ralph does not take the raison slice.
3. Change to: "Ralph placed the three slices in the box," and "Three pieces, he could hold all in one hand"
4. Change to: "Ralph placed the slices in the box," and "Three pieces, he could hold them in one hand"

"bread and been toasted"
Should be had

“OK”
(This is located after "But you have to be willing to listen, OK?”)
Should there be a period?

"He took a slice of the bread, put in the toaster, and said…"
Add "it" after in.

…“Could you get for me?”
The meaning is unclear, if it was supposed to be "get me for me," the toaster is already on the table, Seth left the room for no reason?

"pieces measurement equipment"
Add "of" after pieces
Or: pieces of measuring equipment

Additionally, there are some issues of clarity:
Additionally, there are some issues of clarity:

Note that the first 2 points below do not need to be explained. Ambiguity is fine of that is what you are going for.

Did CIT contain all SCP's after defeating the Foundation?

Is everyone obsessed with toast because of the toaster? Or because CIT rules the world? If it is the toaster, why was Ralph not affected?

Shouldn't they have told Ralph to refer to the toaster in order to activate its effects?

It is mentioned in the comments that the poem writer is an omniscient narrator, but that was not clear to me, I had wondered if they were in universe.

I don't get the title.

Possible spoiler?
Possible spoiler?

Is it implied that the toaster can no longer toast bread? That is ambiguous. Also, just pointing this out: if you remove the last poem, it is ambiguous whether Ralph merged with the toaster rather than escaping.

Also, for fun I wrote part of the above critique and spoiler referring to the toaster in the first person, than changed it afterwards for clarity.

Original version
Original version

"Could you get for me?”
The meaning is unclear, if it was supposed to be "get me for me," I am already on the table, Seth left the room for no reason?
Is everyone obsessed with toast because of me? Or because CIT rules the world? If it is me, why was Ralph not affected?
Shouldn't they have told Ralph to refer to me in order to activate my effects?
Is it implied that I can no longer toast bread? That is ambiguous. Also, if you remove the last poem, it is ambiguous whether Ralph merged with me.

This one had me grinning throughout. I've always felt 426 was a little under-utilized. I can totally see how this would "convert" most benders pretty quickly. Going from "I am a toaster" to "I AM a toaster is such a small but significant jump. Unfortunately, they found the one person who really hates toast in this sliced-and-singed-bread world of yours.

The format tweaks make the poetry more of an intermission; works great for me.

+1, though the title had me thinking this would revolve around Dr. King…

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
As commented on chat, Waterfire, this is a neat, clean piece with a fun representation of another seemingly silly dystopia. It's not exactly my cup of tea, but it held me and made me enjoy its absurd but innerly coherent plot; as a reader, there is nothing else I can ask for.

However, it is somewhat weaker than other stories present in the contest. The main character does bring strong feelings to the table, and I'd love to read more about it, but the use of the Toaster's "POV poetry" as a mellow info-dump could have been handled differently, I guess. For instance, format tweaks in this sense could have made the tale more attractive… then again, that is my answer for everything these days, so I might be wrong.

However, when it comes down to it, it's still good and I'll happily upvote it after the contest.

item.content:encoded:
I actually didn't intend for the exposition to actually be coming from the toaster. This is indicated a few times. It's intended to just be narration.

The rhyming thing is just something I like to do when writing poetry. I don't want to use a specific meter, but I feel that adding transient rhymes helps to keep it feeling… poetic.

As for the method they have for reality benders? They basically started from scratch when they first dealt with them, and the toaster worked, so they kept using it.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
In a different iteration, I may have no-voted this one. I've grown tired of the toaster over the years as it's referenced over and over, and I would have had a hard time supporting something based on it. That's my own issue, though, and I don't know that I could bring myself to downvote based on personal toaster-fatigue. Also, the toast-obsessed society is kind of funny, especially from the point of view of a guy who doesn't like toast.

Two things stick out to me, though, that force my hand. The first, more minor issue, is the ending. Somewhat unexpectedly to myself, I thought of the old tale where Clef is doing the seminar on reality benders, which basically boils down to "shoot them in the head before they know what's up." Given that these guys seem to have dealt with reality benders1 previously, I had an extremely difficult time believing that they would be all like "okay, cool, have fun doing parlor tricks" and then walk away when they could have easily just capped him when he wasn't a threat. This development strikes me as not really making a whole lot of sense from the point of view of the characters involved.

The second, more major issue, is the verse. Firstly, I think those parts could have been cut out entirely, and the story wouldn't have suffered. You've already got an expository device in the newly-promoted assistant, and the toaster itself doesn't really reveal anything that we don't get from Brindis as the story unfolds. The piece was solid enough that the world you constructed was, I think, capable of speaking for itself to the reader.

The verse itself also was problematic for me. I've expounded at great length previously on why I don't think poetry is well-suited to the wiki, and if you want I can tolstoy that again, but suffice to say that I think that a magic toaster is not really a subject suitable for that deeply personal medium. Also, you've chosen to do free verse, but not really, as there's a sort of half-baked rhyme scheme in there that comes and goes. This results in something that doesn't really scan well when I read it, and it produces a dissonant, disjointed feeling that one should really try to avoid when doing poetry.

These two issues are pretty hard to separate from the parts that I liked about the piece, to the point that I think on balance it doesn't really hang together.

Footnotes
1. I'll also take this opportunity to once again beat the dead horse of "there has to be a better term to use than 'reality bender' for these people"
